stimuli.title: Seven people live on different floors of a seven-storey building. Floor 1 is the bottom floor, and floor 7 is the top floor.
stimuli.body:
Clues:
1. In the stated ordering, Tarun comes before Shreya, and Shreya comes before Esha.
2. Rohan is exactly 3 positions above Ira.
3. Harish is exactly 2 positions above Wami.
4. Esha is at floor 4.
stimuli.solution: floor 1: Tarun; floor 2: Shreya; floor 3: Ira; floor 4: Esha; floor 5: Wami; floor 6: Rohan; floor 7: Harish

stimuli.title: In a certain coded language, each word has one unique code.
stimuli.body:
almond violet temple = fi di ve
bridge violet yellow = di ni zu
almond pearl bridge = sa ni ve
temple pearl yellow = sa fi zu
stimuli.solution: violet=di, almond=ve, temple=fi, bridge=ni, yellow=zu, pearl=sa

questions.stem: Given the inequality chain P < X > U ≤ Q ≥ W, decide which conclusions follow. I: P < W. II: P = U.
options: Both conclusions I and II follow
Either conclusion I or II follows
questions.explanation: Exhaustive valid-order checking confirms: I is not necessarily true and II is not necessarily true.

questions.stem: Given the inequality chain P ≤ U < R < T = Z, decide which conclusions follow. I: P ≤ Z. II: R > Z.
options: Both conclusions I and II follow
Either conclusion I or II follows
questions.explanation: Exhaustive valid-order checking confirms: I is always true and II is not necessarily true.

questions.stem: Given the inequality chain Z ≤ V ≥ U ≥ W < R, decide which conclusions follow. I: U = W. II: W < R.
options: Both conclusions I and II follow
Either conclusion I or II follows
questions.explanation: Exhaustive valid-order checking confirms: I is not necessarily true and II is always true.

questions.stem: Given the inequality chain U ≤ W ≥ S = T > X, decide which conclusions follow. I: U ≥ S. II: U ≤ S.
options: Both conclusions I and II follow
Either conclusion I or II follows
questions.explanation: Exhaustive valid-order checking confirms: I is not necessarily true and II is not necessarily true.

questions.stem: Given the inequality chain V = S = R ≤ W ≤ T, decide which conclusions follow. I: R = T. II: V ≥ R.
options: Both conclusions I and II follow
Either conclusion I or II follows
questions.explanation: Exhaustive valid-order checking confirms: I is not necessarily true and II is always true.

questions.stem: Statements: No singers are teachers. All farmers are teachers. Some farmers are teachers. Conclusions: I. No singers are farmers. II. Some farmers are not singers. Which conclusion follows?
options: Both conclusions I and II follow
Either conclusion I or II follows
questions.explanation: All C members belong to B, disjoint from A; some C are explicitly given.

questions.stem: Statements: Some runners are pilots. Some pilots are bakers. Conclusions: I. Some runners are bakers. II. All bakers are runners. Which conclusion follows?
options: Both conclusions I and II follow
Either conclusion I or II follows
questions.explanation: The specified intersections do not force A and C to overlap or include one another.

questions.stem: Statements: Some artists are farmers. All farmers are workers. Conclusions: I. Some artists are workers. II. All artists are workers. Which conclusion follows?
options: Both conclusions I and II follow
Either conclusion I or II follows
questions.explanation: Some A–B members must be C; not all A need be C.

questions.stem: Statements: No drivers are workers. Some workers are pilots. Conclusions: I. Some pilots are not drivers. II. No pilots are drivers. Which conclusion follows?
options: Both conclusions I and II follow
Either conclusion I or II follows
questions.explanation: The B∩C members are outside A; other C members remain unrestricted.

questions.stem: Statements: All farmers are runners. No runners are bakers. Conclusions: I. No farmers are bakers. II. Some farmers are bakers. Which conclusion follows?
options: Both conclusions I and II follow
Either conclusion I or II follows
questions.explanation: A is contained in B, while B and C are disjoint.

questions.stem: Ritu walks 35 km north, then 28 km east, then 7 km south and finally 7 km west. What is her shortest distance from the starting point?
questions.explanation: Net north = 28 km and east = 21 km. Distance = √(28²+21²) = 35 km.

questions.stem: Kiran moves 7 km north, 42 km east, 21 km south and 7 km west. In which direction is Kiran from the start?

questions.stem: A cyclist travels 63 km north, 28 km east, 35 km south and 7 km west. What total distance did the cyclist travel?

questions.stem: Compare x and y. Equation I: x² − 1x − 2 = 0. Equation II: y² + 4y + 3 = 0. Which option is always correct?
questions.explanation: Roots of x are -1 and 2; roots of y are -3 and -1. Hence x ≥ y.

questions.stem: Compare x and y. Equation I: x² + 9x + 20 = 0. Equation II: y² + 1y + 0 = 0. Which option is always correct?
questions.explanation: Roots of x are -5 and -4; roots of y are -1 and 0. Hence x < y.

questions.stem: Compare x and y. Equation I: x² + 4x + 3 = 0. Equation II: y² − 1y − 2 = 0. Which option is always correct?

questions.stem: Compare x and y. Equation I: x² + 3x − 10 = 0. Equation II: y² + 3y + 0 = 0. Which option is always correct?

questions.stem: Compare x and y. Equation I: x² − 3x + 2 = 0. Equation II: y² + 7y + 12 = 0. Which option is always correct?
questions.explanation: Roots of x are 1 and 2; roots of y are -4 and -3. Hence x > y.
